q: The technician opens the battery lockers of the catamaran and shows you this. What do you want to be sure of before he closes them?
a: That each engine has its own starter battery and the house bank is separate from both
o: That all five batteries are wired as one bank, for the most capacity
That the house bank starts the engines when the starter batteries are low
That the port engine battery also runs the fridge, being the strongest one
why: Separate banks: a flat house bank after a night at anchor still leaves each engine its own battery to start.

q: The technician shows you the battery switches and gives you this advice. How will you actually run them?
a: ENGINE and HOUSE on at sea and at anchor; BOTH only for a flat-battery start; all off leaving the boat
o: BOTH on all week, as he says, so the fridge and the lights can draw on both banks together
HOUSE off under way so the alternator puts the whole charge into the engine battery
ENGINE off at anchor so the fridge and the lights cannot flatten the starter battery
why: Both banks on keeps them separate; BOTH joins them, so a flat house bank takes the engine battery with it.

fig.title: Battery switches
lines: Technician: "just leave BOTH on all week"

q: First morning at anchor; you read the battery monitor before switching anything on. What state is the house bank in?
a: Full — a rested bank at 12.7 V is near 100 %
o: Half — 12.7 V is midway between flat and full
Flat — anything under 13 V needs the engine now
Overcharged — a bank at rest should read 12.0 V
why: Rested, no load: 12.7 V full, 12.4 V about 75 %, 12.2 V half, 12.0 V or less flat.

q: At check-in the technician points at the voltmeter and says the batteries are 'perfect'. What does this reading actually tell you?
a: Only that the charger is working — the state of the bank shows after a rest off the charger
o: That the bank is full and will hold 13.8 V all night at anchor
That the bank is being overcharged and the charger must go off now
That the batteries are new — an old bank never gets up to 13.8 V
why: On charge the charger sets the volts (13.8 float, 14.4 bulk); the bank's own voltage is read after an hour at rest.

q: You are going through the panel with the technician and see this. What do you do?
a: Note it on the form and ask the base to sort it before you sail — the charger is off or the bank is dead
o: Accept it — the bank will come up once you run the engine on Sunday morning
Switch to BOTH so the engine battery carries the house bank for the week
Move the cable to another pedestal socket, see the light come on and sign
why: Plugged in, the bank should read 13.8–14.4 V; 11.8 V with current going out means no charge — and ask how old the bank is.

q: The technician waves at the panel, says 'all the usual' and heads for the engine bay. What do you ask him to do first?
a: Switch on each breaker in turn and show you what it feeds
o: Leave every breaker on so you can find out as you go
Explain the 230 V side only — the 12 V side is obvious
Hand you the boat manual to read the panel on passage
why: You will be finding these at night in a blow; VHF, instruments and the windlass each have their own breaker.

q: Your crew asks whether the kettle and the hairdryer will work in the bays. What do you tell them?
a: Only on shore power — at anchor the 230 V outlets are dead and the inverter runs a laptop, not a kettle
o: Yes — flip the 230 V main breaker and the batteries feed the outlets directly
Yes with the engine running — the alternator powers the 230 V side of the panel
Yes — switch the charger on and it converts 12 V into 230 V for the outlets
why: The 230 V side is live only on shore power or a generator; a 300 W inverter will not run a 2 kW kettle.

fig.title: Main panel
lines: Right: 230 V AC — RCD, charger, outlets, water heater
Inverter 300 W: one socket at the chart table

q: The technician plugs the shore cable in and goes to fetch the inventory list. You look at the 230 V panel. What do you do?
a: Unplug it and tell the base — the pedestal is miswired; no 230 V until it is fixed
o: Press the RCD test button to clear the warning and carry on
Ignore it — polarity only matters on American 110 V boats
Turn the plug the other way round in the pedestal socket
why: Reverse polarity leaves the live side on breakers that should be neutral; an RCD does not make it safe.

q: Sunday 10:00, the technician has gone and you are ready to cast off from the pontoon. In what order do you deal with the shore power?
a: Charger and 230 V main off, pedestal switch off, unplug the pedestal end first, then the boat end, stow the cable
o: Unplug the boat end first, hand the live cable to a crew on the pontoon, then the pedestal end
Leave it plugged in until the engine is running for a last charge, then pull both ends at once
Pull both ends, leave the cable on the pontoon for the base to collect, cast off
why: Dead before you touch it, pedestal end first so no live plug lies on deck; the cable is on the inventory.

q: You ask the technician to start the engine and watch the battery monitor. What do you tell him?
a: It is not charging — the alternator or belt needs looking at before you leave
o: All good — volts must drop a little when the engine takes its load
All good — the alternator only starts charging above 2000 rpm
All good — it charges the engine battery, which is not on this monitor
why: With the engine running the monitor should show about 14 V and current going in; 12.3 V and −8 A is no charge.

q: The technician resets the breaker, the windlass runs, and he moves on. What rule do you take away, and what do you ask before he goes?
a: Engine running whenever you use it; and where the spare fuses are, for anything that blows instead of tripping
o: Breaker on all week so the remote always works; and whether the base will come out if it trips again
Use it with the engine off at anchor so the alternator is unloaded; and the make of the motor
Start the engine only if it stalls; and whether the house bank can be switched in to help it
why: The windlass draws 80–100 A; the alternator covers it and the engine is ready. A breaker resets, a fuse needs a spare.

fig.title: Windlass
lines: Breaker 80 A at the chart table
Tripped on the first test, reset

q: Evening in the bay, the fridge is the only thing running. Do you leave it on overnight?
a: Yes — about 5 A for 10 h is 50 Ah, a quarter of the bank; charge with the engine in the morning
o: No — switch it off at night; 5 A will flatten 200 Ah well before dawn
Yes, and the lights and the inverter too — 200 Ah is enough for the week
Only with BOTH selected so the engine battery shares the night's load
why: Amps × hours = amp-hours; a lead-acid bank should not go below half, so 50 Ah of 200 is fine.

q: Saturday night you switch on NAV LIGHTS and walk out along the pontoon to look at the bow. This is what you see. What do you do?
a: Note the dead starboard light on the form and ask the base to replace the bulb before you sail
o: Sail with the tricolour instead — it shows the same arcs
Buy a bulb in town on Monday and fit it yourself
Accept it — you plan to be in a harbour every night
why: Test the lights at the pontoon, at night, from outside; the base replaces what is dead.

fig.note: Pontoon, 21:00 — seen from ahead, NAV LIGHTS on

q: You switch on the ANCHOR breaker and look up from the pontoon. What have you confirmed?
a: The all-round white anchor light works — the one to show every night at anchor
o: The steaming light works — the one to show at anchor with the engine off
The tricolour works — show it at anchor to save the battery
The deck light works — enough for a quiet bay with no traffic
why: At anchor at night a vessel shows an all-round white light (Rule 30); test it where you can see it.

q: The technician reads this off the inventory list without opening the floor. How do you check it before you sign?
a: Switch to ON and hear it run, lift the float for AUTO, find the hand-pump handle
o: Trust the panel light — it only comes on if the pump is wired
Leave it on AUTO and look at the bilge again at check-out
Set it to OFF so it cannot drain the batteries at anchor
why: A pump that was never heard is a pump that may not run; AUTO stays selected all week.

fig.title: Bilge pump
lines: Electric: float switch in the bilge
Hand pump in the cockpit, handle in the locker

q: What do you do with these two before you sign, and what do you ask?
a: Press TEST on each and hear it; ask what to do when the gas alarm sounds
o: Take the battery out of the CO alarm so it does not chirp at night
Note that they are fitted — testing them trips the panel breaker
Ask for a spare detector in case this one goes off falsely
why: Gas alarm: close the bottle valve, no switches, ventilate; a dead CO alarm goes on the form.

fig.title: Alarms
lines: Gas detector: sensor in the bilge, panel at the galley
CO alarm in the saloon, 9 V battery

q: The technician says 'you will not need these' and skips them. What do you ask him to show you anyway?
a: The solar controller charging, and the generator started with water at its exhaust; note the hours
o: Nothing — extras you do not use are not your problem at check-out
The generator fuel level only; a solar panel has nothing to check
The panel wiring under the bimini, with the controller switched off
why: Anything on the inventory is yours for the week; a generator is checked like the engine — hours and raw water.

fig.title: Also fitted
lines: Solar 200 W on the bimini, controller at the chart table
Generator strainer under the aft bunk

q: The technician brings this cable to plug you in. What do you do?
a: Refuse it and ask for another — a damaged 230 V cable on a wet pontoon can kill
o: Tape over the cut and plug in — the RCD will trip if anything leaks
Use it with dry hands and keep the cut end on the boat, not the pontoon
Plug it in only at night when nobody is walking along the pontoon
why: 230 V, seawater and bare copper: no tape, no dry hands; the base has another cable.

fig.title: Shore cable
lines: Outer sheath cut, copper showing near the plug

q: The technician lifts the bunk and shows you the batteries. What do you do?
a: Ask him to show you the master switches and fit terminal covers; you do not touch the terminals
o: Check the terminals are tight with the winch handle while he watches
Note it and plan to buy terminal covers in town on Monday
Ask him to disconnect the bank so you can inspect each battery
why: A dropped spanner across the terminals is a fire; in a fire you must find the master switch in the dark.

fig.title: Battery compartment
lines: Under the aft bunk, terminals uncovered
Master switches: behind the companionway steps
Technician: "check they are tight if you like"

q: The technician asks how you plan to run the boat for the week. What is your plan?
a: Engine an hour morning and evening, fridge on, instruments and autopilot off when not needed
o: Run everything — 200 Ah will see the week out without charging
Keep the engine idling all night so the fridge never drains the bank
Fridge off, autopilot on all night — the autopilot matters more
why: About 100 Ah usable; a day's draw is near that, so charge twice a day and cut what is not in use.

fig.title: Power budget
lines: Fridge 5 A · instruments 2 A · lights 2 A · autopilot 4 A

q: Tuesday, 08:00, at anchor. You read the battery monitor before breakfast. What does the third figure tell you?
a: That 76 Ah have been drawn from the bank since it was last full
o: That 76 Ah are left in the bank before it is completely flat
That the bank has lost 76 Ah of its capacity with age
That the alternator will put back 76 Ah in the next hour
why: The monitor counts amp-hours out and in since the last full charge; 76 drawn from 200 Ah matches the 62 %.

lines: Last full: Sunday at the base

q: Saturday night on shore power, a crew member in the aft cabin complains of a humming box under the bunk. You read its display. What do you tell them?
a: It is the charger holding a full bank; the fan hum is normal
o: It is the charger failing; switch it off until the morning
It is the bank still flat; FLOAT means a slow first charge
It is the inverter; it runs whenever shore power is in
why: Bulk, absorption, float: float is the last stage — the bank is full and the charger just keeps it there.

q: Monday, the plotter and the depth go dead together. Behind the panel you find this. What do you fit?
a: A 10 A spare; if it blows again, leave it out and call the base
o: A 15 A spare, so that it does not blow again on the same load
A 20 A spare, since a bigger fuse protects the plotter better
Any spare that fits the holder, since the rating is only a guide
why: A fuse protects the wire; a bigger one lets the wire burn before it blows. A second blow means a fault, not a weak fuse.

fig.title: Fuse holder: INSTRUMENTS
lines: Spares box: 5 A, 10 A, 15 A, 20 A

q: Wednesday, 18:00, you are berthed in a marina in Kos and want shore power. In which order do you connect?
a: Boat end first, then the pedestal end, then the pedestal switch and the 230 V main
o: Pedestal end first and switched on, then carry the live plug to the boat
Boat's 230 V main on first, so the panel is ready when the cable goes live
Both ends at once, one crew at each, then switch the pedestal on
why: Never hold a live plug: the cable goes live last, from the pedestal, once both ends are in.

fig.title: Marina berth
lines: Pedestal: 16 A socket with its own switch
Boat inlet: in the cockpit locker

q: Monday noon in a bay, engine off. You read the solar controller at the chart table. What is it doing?
a: Charging the house bank at 7 A from the panels
o: Nothing yet — 19.5 V is the panels' voltage with no load
Drawing 7 A from the bank to run the controller
Overcharging — a bank should never read above 12.7 V
why: The controller turns the panels' higher voltage into a charge: +7 A is going in, and 13.9 V is a bank on charge.

q: Your crew want to stuff a towel into the small vent by the battery box under the bunk to stop a draught. What do you tell them?
a: Leave it open — batteries on charge give off hydrogen that must get out
o: Fine at anchor — the vent only matters on shore power
Fine — the vent is there only to let the batteries' heat out
Fine — modern batteries are sealed and give off nothing at all
why: Lead-acid batteries gas hydrogen on charge, more when overcharged; with the vent blocked it collects where a spark can light it.

q: Saturday, 18:00, on shore power since noon. You lift the aft bunk and find this. What do you do?
a: Charger off, hatches open, no switches or sparks near it, and call the base
o: Loosen the hot battery's terminals with a spanner and lift it out
Leave it — the smell is the holding tank next to the batteries
Lay a wet towel over it and let the charger finish its cycle
why: A battery cooking on charge gives off hydrogen sulphide and hydrogen: stop the charge, ventilate, no sparks.

fig.title: Battery compartment
lines: One battery hot to the touch, case bulging

q: Wednesday, under sail, engine off. Smoke and a hot smell come from behind the DC panel. What do you do first?
a: Battery switches off, then the powder extinguisher at the panel if it still burns
o: A bucket of seawater on the panel, then the battery switches
Open the panel and find the burning wire before switching off
Switch the breakers off one by one to find the faulty circuit
why: Cut the source first: with the batteries isolated most electrical fires die; never water on a live panel.

fig.title: Chart table
lines: Smoke from behind the DC panel

q: 42 ft catamaran at anchor. A crew member asks to use her hairdryer on the inverter socket. What do you say?
a: Yes, for a few minutes, with the generator or an engine running
o: Yes, as long as she likes — 400 Ah does not notice a hairdryer
No — an inverter cannot run anything that heats up
Only with the charger on, so that it feeds the inverter
why: 1,600 W from 12 V is about 140 A; ten minutes is over 20 Ah — fine with a charge going in, not every morning off the bank.

q: Tuesday, motoring along the coast, the INSTRUMENTS breaker trips. You reset it and it trips again at once. What do you do?
a: Leave it off, navigate by compass and paper chart, and call the base
o: Hold the breaker in by hand until the instruments come back
Tape the breaker on so that a wave cannot trip it again
Move the instruments onto the fridge's 15 A breaker
why: A breaker that trips at once has found a short; forcing it on heats the wiring. Paper chart, compass, and the base's help.

q: The technician shows you the electric winch for the main halyard. What do you ask him before he moves on?
a: Where its isolator is, so anyone can stop it if a hand is caught
o: Whether the button can be held while you go forward to watch the sail
Whether it runs off the starter battery so the house bank is spared
How many turns to put on so that the line can never slip off
why: A powered winch does not feel a finger or a fouled line; the button at the helm and the isolator below must be known to all.

q: Thursday in the marina. Your shore cable sags into the water between the pontoon and the transom, and the crew want to swim off the stern. What do you do?
a: Lift the cable clear and tie it up; nobody swims in the marina
o: Nothing — the RCD on the pedestal makes it safe to swim
Switch the boat's charger off and let them swim
Let them swim on the far side of the boat from the cable
why: Stray 230 V in marina water can kill a swimmer; keep cables out of the water and do not swim between pontoons.

q: Thursday, 15:00, the catamaran at anchor. The generator runs for the air-con and the crew are jumping off the stern steps. What do you do?
a: Stop the generator while anyone is swimming near the stern
o: Nothing — the exhaust goes into the water, not the air
Ask them to swim off the starboard hull only
Run it faster so that the exhaust clears away quicker
why: Generator exhaust carries carbon monoxide; at the stern, in still air, a swimmer breathes it at the waterline. Swim with it off.

fig.title: Catamaran at anchor
lines: Generator running, exhaust at the port transom

q: Monday, 08:00: the starter battery was flat, you switched to BOTH and the engine is now running. What do you do with the switches?
a: BOTH off now, and an hour's charge before you trust the starter alone
o: Leave BOTH on all day so the starter charges from the house bank
BOTH off and stop the engine — it has started, the job is done
Stop the engine and restart it on ENGINE alone to test it
why: Left in parallel, the two banks drain together again overnight; separate them and give the starter time to charge.
ref: Battery switches — after a parallel start

q: Wednesday evening on shore power in Split. Each time the water-heater breaker goes on, the RCD trips. What do you do?
a: Leave the water heater off and tell the base — it is leaking to earth
o: Reset the RCD and hold it up until the water has warmed
Plug into another pedestal socket and try it again
Run the water heater from the inverter instead
why: An RCD trips on current leaking to earth; a heater element that trips it is faulty and could make the water live.

fig.title: 230 V panel
lines: RCD trips when WATER HEATER goes on
Charger and sockets: fine without it

q: Thursday, 08:00, in a marina in Trogir: the pedestal trips each morning as breakfast starts. What is happening, and what do you do?
a: Heater, kettle and charger together pass 10 A — one big load at a time
o: The pedestal is faulty — ask the marina for another berth
The kettle leaks to earth — throw it out and use the stove
Morning damp in the cable — dry the plug and reset it
why: Watts ÷ 230 = amps: 3,700 W is about 16 A on a 10 A pedestal. Water heater off while the kettle boils.

q: Tuesday, a town marina: your plug does not fit the pedestal socket. A crew member offers to cut the plug off and push the bare wires in. What do you do?
a: Ask the marina office for an adapter; no bare wires in a pedestal
o: Let him do it, as long as he switches the pedestal off first
Do it, and tape the wires in so that they cannot pull out
Run an extension lead across from the neighbour's boat
why: Bare wires in a 230 V socket on a wet pontoon can kill, and a cut plug is charged to your deposit; ask the office for an adapter.

fig.title: Pedestal
lines: Sockets: a type your plug does not fit

q: Wednesday, 21:00, at anchor in a bay where boats are still coming in: the anchor light has failed and you cannot fix it tonight. What do you do?
a: Hang an all-round white lamp in the foretriangle and call the base in the morning
o: Go up the mast in the dark and change the bulb
Show the steaming light instead until the morning
Leave the cabin lights on so that boats see the glow
why: The rule wants an all-round white light where it is best seen; a lamp hung forward does that. Nobody climbs the mast at night.

q: Your crew, keen to save power, are about to switch off every breaker for the night at anchor. Which stay on?
a: Anchor light, bilge pump and gas alarm; the rest is your choice
o: Only the fridge — the food matters more than the alarms
None — the bilge pump runs straight off the battery
Anchor light only — the gas alarm has its own battery
why: Seen, kept afloat, warned of gas: these three keep the boat safe overnight; the fridge or the VHF is a choice.

fig.title: DC panel
lines: ANCHOR LIGHT · BILGE PUMP · GAS ALARM

q: You shine a torch on the starter battery while the technician waits. What do you ask for?
a: The post cleaned and the lug tightened before you sail
o: A tin of grease, so you can clean it yourself on Monday
Nothing — the crust is normal on a working battery
A note on the form, and you will take it from there
why: A loose, corroded lug fails under the starter's load — the engine will not turn on the very morning you need it.

fig.title: Starter battery
lines: White-green crust on the positive post

q: 42 ft catamaran with a lithium house bank, Tuesday evening at anchor. Your crew say the volts 'look fine'. What do you tell them?
a: Trust the 25 % — a lithium bank stays near 13 V until it is almost empty
o: Trust the 13.1 V — the percentage is only the monitor's guess
Both are fine — 13.1 V on any bank means three-quarters full
Neither — read the starter battery to judge the house bank
why: Lithium holds a flat 13.0–13.3 V over most of its charge, so the volts say little; the monitor's amp-hour count is the gauge.

q: Wednesday on the catamaran, a long calm passage under power; you decide to run one engine to save fuel. Which one?
a: The starboard — only its alternator charges the house bank
o: The port — its alternator has less to charge, so it lasts longer
Either — each alternator charges every battery aboard
Swap every hour so that both starters stay equally charged
why: On many cats only one engine charges the house bank, and the base's sheet says which; run the other and the fridge sits on a falling bank.

fig.title: Catamaran charging (base's sheet)
lines: Stbd alternator: stbd starter + house bank

q: Sunday evening at anchor you find the inverter on with nothing plugged in; your crew left it 'just in case'. What do you tell them?
a: Off unless something is plugged in — idling, it takes about 24 Ah a day
o: Leave it — with nothing plugged in it draws nothing
Leave it — at anchor it keeps the house bank topped up
Leave it — switching it on and off wears out its fan
why: An inverter draws power just standing by; a day of idling is over a tenth of a 200 Ah bank, for nothing.

q: Motoring out of the bay, a crew member tidying the chart table turns the ENGINE battery switch off 'because the alternator is running now'. What do you do?
a: Switch it back on at once — cutting it with the engine running can wreck the alternator
o: Leave it — once running, a diesel needs no battery at all
Leave it, and switch it back on before you stop the engine
Switch it back on only if the battery light comes on
why: With the battery cut the alternator's output has nowhere to go; the spike can blow its diodes. Battery switches stay on under way.

q: Monday, 07:00, in a bay. The fridge was the only thing on overnight. You compare the readings. What do you do?
a: The bank has lost much of its capacity — call the base for new batteries on your route
o: Nothing — a fridge always takes a bank down to 11.9 V by morning
Switch the fridge off each night and carry on with the plan
Run the engine all day; a full charge will restore the old bank
why: 40 Ah from 200 should still read about 12.4 V; 11.9 V means the old bank holds far less than its label. The base can swap it midweek.

q: Catamaran, three nights at anchor planned. Reading the power figures at the briefing, what do you decide?
a: Cockpit fridge off and an engine run twice a day — 12 A round the clock outruns the sun
o: All three on — 400 Ah and the solar will cover any week at anchor
Solar alone will do — 400 W is more than the fridges use
Freezer off, nothing else — the fridges barely draw at night
why: 12 A × 24 h is about 290 Ah a day; 100 Ah of sun and 200 usable last about a day. Cut a load and charge twice a day.

fig.title: Catamaran 42 ft — power budget
lines: Galley fridge, cockpit fridge, freezer: 12 A together
Solar 400 W: about 100 Ah on a sunny day

q: Thursday evening in a bay: strong wind is forecast for Friday's passage back to the base. You read this. What do you do tonight?
a: Charge it full tonight and in the morning — tomorrow everything runs on it
o: Save the engine for tomorrow — it will charge on the way back
Switch the house bank off tonight to hold it at 55 %
Nothing — the starter battery takes over if the house runs low
why: Go into a blow with a full bank: autopilot, plotter, VHF and bilge pump all draw on it, and the engine may yet stop.

fig.title: Thursday 19:00
lines: Friday: F6–7, 25 miles to the base
Autopilot, VHF, plotter, bilge pump: house bank

q: Saturday 14:00, shore power off since the morning cleaning. The technician says 'the monitor says full'. What do you do?
a: Believe the volts — have the bank tested and the monitor reset before you sign
o: Believe the monitor — it counts every amp, the voltmeter only guesses
Accept it — 12.1 V with the fridge running is a full bank
Plug the charger back in for an hour, see 100 % again and sign
why: A monitor that has lost count shows whatever it was last set to; 12.1 V under a small load is a bank near half or below.

q: Tuesday, 02:00, at anchor: a hum under the saloon floor wakes you. You find this. What do you do?
a: Pump to OFF, look in the bilge every few hours, and call the base in the morning
o: Leave it on AUTO — better a pump running dry than a flooded bilge
Pull its fuse for the rest of the week, since the bilge is dry
Set it to ON so that it runs steadily rather than cycling
why: A pump running dry burns out and drains the bank; switch it off and check the bilge by hand until the base fixes the float.

fig.title: Bilge
lines: Bilge pump running, panel light on
Float switch stuck up, will not free

q: Wednesday, 11:00, motoring between islands, you check the monitor. What do you do for the rest of the week?
a: Call the base, make for a marina with shore power tonight, and cut every load you can
o: Carry on — the house bank will last till Friday on its own
Tighten the belt hard yourself and keep motoring as planned
Switch to BOTH so that the starter battery charges the house
why: No charge means the bank only falls; the base can send a technician, and shore power keeps the fridge and lights going until then.

lines: Battery light on since this morning
